title: The act of contrition
hookLine: sorry because of love, not only fear, and a promise to try again
last: THE HARDEST PART IS THE DOOR.

cards: Two kids break a neighbor's window with a baseball. The first says sorry because his dad is standing right there with that look.
The second says sorry because she likes the old man next door; she can see his face at the broken window, and it hurts her that she did that to him. Both apologies count. But they aren't the same.
One is sorry about getting caught. The other is sorry about the person. Catholics have an old word for this, and a prayer to go with it.

teach.b: Contrition comes from the Latin conterere, to grind down, to crush, like grain between stones. A contrite heart has been broken open.
The Psalms use the picture: in the Douay-Rheims, "a contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise." Catholic teaching names two kinds of sorrow, a lot like those two kids.

Sorrow out of love for God, because sin hurts someone who is good, is called perfect contrition. Sorrow because of what sin does, its ugliness or fear of its consequences, is imperfect contrition, or attrition.
Here's the merciful part: the Church teaches that imperfect sorrow is enough to begin with, inside the sacrament. You don't have to feel exactly the right thing before you walk in.
Near the end of confession, the penitent says an act of contrition. One traditional version begins: "O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended thee."

teach.h: SORRY FROM LOVE, OR FROM FEAR.
teach.b: It names both kinds of sorrow, fear and love, and ends with a firm resolve, with God's help, to sin no more and to avoid what leads to it. That resolve matters.
Without it, sorrow is only a feeling; with it, sorrow becomes a turn. And you don't have to use the memorized version.

teach.h: O MY GOD, I AM HEARTILY SORRY.
teach.b: The Church allows an act of contrition in your own words, as long as it says you're sorry and you mean to try again.

teach.h: IN YOUR OWN WORDS IS FINE.
teach.b: Look at Peter after he denied Jesus three times.
The Douay-Rheims says simply: "And Peter going out, wept bitterly." He didn't give up. He came back.

how: Near the end of confession Catholics pray an act of contrition, often the traditional one learned as children, or in their own words, and some also pray one each night.

games.q: you're Peter. you've just denied knowing Jesus three times, and the rooster crows. what do you do?
games.why: "And Peter going out, wept bitterly." real sorrow, and not the end: he came back, and later led the Church.

practice: Bring back the one thing from your look back two days ago, or something new, and ask who it hurt; picture their face, and let the sorry be about them, not about how you look. Then find one small thing you'll do differently.
If you pray, tell God both in your own words, as simple as you like; if you don't, say them to yourself: I'm sorry, and I'll try.

wordCard.voice: Contrition. From the Latin for crushed. Sorrow for sin, best when it comes from love, always joined to a promise to try again. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: to grind or crush. Its past participle contritus gave us contrite.

carryVoice: Your line: sorry, and resolved. Sorry about the person, not only about getting caught. Day one hundred thirty-five, done.
